concepts.name: LAF: Architecture and Institutional Purpose
key_dimensions: Definition as a monetary policy tool vs. a liquidity management tool — dual role trap
Introduced by RBI in 2000 based on Narasimham Committee recommendations — historical anchor
Distinction between LAF as a corridor system vs. a single-rate mechanism
Role in transmitting monetary policy signals to short-term money markets

concepts.name: Repo Rate: Mechanics and Signaling Function
key_dimensions: Repo as RBI injecting liquidity vs. banks borrowing — direction of flow trap
Repo rate as the policy rate and its position as the floor/ceiling in the corridor — common confusion
Collateral requirement (government securities) and its implications for credit creation
Repo rate vs. Bank Rate: differences in purpose, tenure, and penal applicability

concepts.name: Reverse Repo Rate: Absorption Mechanism
key_dimensions: Reverse repo as RBI absorbing excess liquidity — conceptual reversal trap
Reverse repo rate historically set 100 bps below repo; now effectively replaced by SDF — critical update
Role in setting the lower bound of the LAF corridor
Why excess liquidity parked at reverse repo does not earn as much as lending — incentive design

concepts.name: Marginal Standing Facility (MSF): Emergency Liquidity Window
key_dimensions: MSF rate set 25 bps above repo rate — forms the upper bound/ceiling of the LAF corridor
Allows banks to borrow beyond their SLR holdings (up to a limit) — unique feature vs. repo
Overnight borrowing only — contrast with term repo under LAF
MSF vs. Repo: who accesses MSF and under what conditions — UPSC trap on eligibility and purpose

concepts.name: Standing Deposit Facility (SDF): New Floor of LAF Corridor
key_dimensions: Introduced in April 2022 Union Budget and operationalized in MPC meeting — recency trap
SDF rate set 25 bps below repo rate, replacing reverse repo as the effective floor
Key distinction: SDF is uncollateralized (RBI does not provide securities) vs. reverse repo which is collateralized
Why SDF is superior to reverse repo for absorbing large surplus liquidity — Basel III and collateral scarcity angle

concepts.name: LAF Corridor: Structure and Width
key_dimensions: Corridor defined: SDF rate (floor) → Repo rate (policy rate) → MSF rate (ceiling) — post-2022 structure
Symmetric vs. asymmetric corridor debates and RBI's historical shifts
Corridor width (currently ±25 bps) and its implications for interest rate volatility in call money markets
Pre-2022 corridor trap: Reverse repo was floor; SDF now replaced it — examinees often miss this update

concepts.name: Liquidity Conditions: Surplus vs. Deficit Modes
key_dimensions: Deficit liquidity: banks borrow from RBI via repo/MSF — repo rate becomes the operative rate
Surplus liquidity: banks park funds with RBI via SDF — SDF rate becomes the operative rate
Structural vs. frictional liquidity — RBI's classification and policy implications
COVID-era surplus liquidity and RBI's challenge in managing inflation through LAF — recent context

concepts.name: Weighted Average Call Rate (WACR) and LAF Transmission
key_dimensions: WACR as the operating target of monetary policy — not repo rate itself, a common misconception
How LAF corridor anchors WACR within the band — transmission mechanism
Deviation of WACR from repo rate as a measure of liquidity stress
WACR vs. MIBOR vs. T-Bill rate — overlapping benchmarks and their distinctions

concepts.name: Variable Rate Repo (VRR) and Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR)
key_dimensions: Fixed rate vs. variable rate operations under LAF — auction-based mechanism
VRR used for injecting liquidity at market-determined rates; VRRR for absorbing
Why RBI shifted to VRRR as the primary tool during 2021–22 surplus liquidity phase
Term VRRR vs. Overnight VRRR — tenure flexibility and its signaling effect

concepts.name: Open Market Operations (OMO) vs. LAF: Complementarity and Distinction
key_dimensions: LAF manages short-term/daily liquidity; OMO manages durable/structural liquidity — critical distinction
OMO involves outright purchase/sale of G-secs; LAF involves repurchase agreements — instrument difference
Operation Twist as a special OMO — UPSC frequently tests this overlap
When RBI uses OMO alongside LAF — policy coordination trap

concepts.name: Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) Interaction with LAF
key_dimensions: CRR changes affect systemic liquidity that LAF then fine-tunes — sequencing of tools
CRR cut vs. repo rate cut — different transmission channels and speed
CRR balances maintained at RBI do not earn interest — contrast with SDF which does earn interest
COVID-era CRR cut and its interaction with LAF surplus — practical case study

concepts.name: Monetary Policy Transmission Through LAF
key_dimensions: Transmission chain: Repo rate → WACR → MCLR/EBLR → Lending rates — steps and lags
Why transmission is asymmetric (faster for rate hikes than cuts) — behavioral angle
External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR) and its direct link to repo rate — improved transmission
MCLR vs. EBLR: which transmits LAF changes more efficiently and why

concepts.name: Eligible Collateral and Counterparties Under LAF
key_dimensions: Only scheduled commercial banks (including foreign banks) can access LAF — cooperative banks and NBFCs excluded, a common trap
Eligible securities: Government of India dated securities, Treasury Bills, State Development Loans
Haircut concept on collateral — risk management angle
Primary dealers' access to MSF — a frequently missed exception

concepts.name: LAF and Inflation Targeting: MPC Interface
key_dimensions: MPC sets the repo rate (policy rate); RBI operationalizes it through LAF — institutional separation of decision and execution
Flexible Inflation Targeting framework (4±2%) and how LAF rate changes signal MPC stance
Neutral, accommodative, and withdrawal of accommodation stances — how each affects LAF operations
Conflict scenario: high inflation but banking sector stress — LAF design to handle both simultaneously

concepts.name: LAF, Exchange Rate, and Capital Flows
key_dimensions: Tight LAF (high repo) attracts capital inflows — rupee appreciation pressure
Impossible Trinity: RBI cannot simultaneously control exchange rate, capital flows, and interest rate via LAF
Forex intervention by RBI creates rupee liquidity that LAF must sterilize — sterilization trap
Market Stabilization Scheme (MSS) as a sterilization tool complementary to LAF — overlap distinction

concepts.name: Historical Evolution of LAF in India
key_dimensions: Pre-LAF regime: CRR and sector-specific refinance windows — why LAF was a reform
Narasimham Committee II (1998) recommendation → LAF introduced June 2000
2011 revision: LAF made a purely overnight window; term repos introduced separately
2020 onwards: Surplus liquidity management challenges and eventual SDF introduction in 2022 — timeline trap

concepts.name: Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) Banks and LAF Access Restrictions
key_dimensions: Banks under PCA framework may face restrictions on certain borrowing windows — governance overlap
RBI's discretion in limiting LAF access for financially stressed banks
Whether PCA restrictions override a bank's statutory right to access LAF — legal dimension
Relationship between weak bank balance sheets and poor LAF transmission — systemic risk angle

concepts.name: LAF vs. Bank Rate: Conceptual Traps
key_dimensions: Bank Rate is now aligned to MSF rate (both currently same) — post-2012 alignment, a major trap
Bank Rate applies to penal interest on CRR shortfalls; repo is for routine liquidity — functional difference
Bank Rate is a signaling rate with no collateral requirement; repo requires G-sec collateral
Historical Bank Rate as long-term refinance rate vs. current ceremonial/penal role

concepts.name: Durable Liquidity vs. Transient Liquidity Management
key_dimensions: LAF addresses transient/frictional liquidity (daily mismatches); OMO/CRR address durable liquidity
RBI's liquidity management framework post-2014 Urjit Patel Committee — conceptual restructuring
Liquidity Neutral stance as an RBI objective — what it means and how LAF is calibrated for it
Seasonal factors (advance tax outflows, GST payments, crop procurement) creating transient stress managed via LAF

concepts.name: LAF in the Context of Government Borrowing and G-Sec Market
key_dimensions: Government securities as the backbone of LAF collateral — sovereign debt and monetary policy linkage
Ways and Means Advances (WMA) to government vs. LAF to banks — both use G-secs but different counterparties
When heavy G-sec supply tightens system liquidity and forces banks to repo more — fiscal-monetary nexus
RBI's dual role as debt manager and monetary authority creating potential conflict in LAF rate setting
